From Typewriting to Variable Fonts:
History, Technology, and Contemporary Letter Design
Authors: Scriptum, ChatGPT, Google, Wikipedia
Introduction

Typewriting is both a mechanical craft and a cultural practice. For more than a century, the rhythmic clatter of typebars striking paper defined office work, literary production, and personal correspondence. Today, most people "type" on glass screens or plastic keyboards instead of cast-iron machines, yet the underlying idea remains the same: turning finger movements into reproducible written language. This essay traces the historical development of typewriting from early mechanical typewriters to electric models and digital word processors. 
It then examines the "state of the art" in letter design, focusing on OpenType technology, variable fonts, color fonts, and contemporary trends in typography. The journey from Remington typewriters to responsive web typography shows how a seemingly old-fashioned technology continues to shape how we read, write, and design text today.
Early Experiments and the Birth of the Typewriter

Attempts to mechanize writing predate the modern typewriter by centuries. Inventors in eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century Europe experimented with devices that could produce legible text more quickly than handwriting, often inspired by printing presses or music instruments. Most of these machines were prototypes or curiosities, and none achieved wide adoption. The breakthrough came in the #s and #s with the work of Christopher Latham Sholes and his collaborators in Milwaukee. Their machine, known as the Sholes and Glidden typewriter and later marketed as the Remington No. #, became the first commercially successful typewriter.

It introduced key elements that would define the industry: a cylindrical platen to hold the paper, a keyboard with four banks of keys, and an internal system of typebars that struck an inked ribbon against the paper. It was also the first widely marketed machine to use the QWERTY layout, which arranged keys to reduce jams in the typebar mechanism and ultimately became the dominant keyboard layout for typewriters and later computers.
Despite its innovations, the Sholes and Glidden had limitations. It could only type uppercase letters, and it was a "blind writer" the typed text was hidden beneath the carriage, forcing typists to trust that the machine was printing correctly. Even so, as Remington scaled up production and partnered with dedicated sales agencies, typewriters moved from novelty to essential office equipment.
Standardization, Visible Writing, and Social Effects

In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, competing manufacturers refined typewriter design. New models added the shift key, allowing the same typebars to produce both uppercase and lowercase letters. Others introduced "visible writing" mechanisms so that typists could see the text as it was produced, improving speed and accuracy. By the early #s, typewriters had converged on a broadly familiar form: a keyboard, a carriage with a platen, a return lever, and a ribbon mechanism.

Standardization in typewriter design reshaped business communication. Typewritten documents offered uniform appearance and high legibility, which was particularly valuable in rapidly expanding corporations. The typewriter also had deep social implications. It opened new professional opportunities for women as typists, stenographers, and secretaries. In many Western countries, the proportion of women in clerical jobs rose sharply between the #s and the early twentieth century. For many, learning to type represented a path to relatively better pay and working conditions than factory labor.
At the same time, typewriting influenced writing itself. Authors such as Mark Twain, who famously submitted one of the first typewritten manuscripts, discovered that the machine changed their relationship to the text. The consistent letterforms, lack of handwriting idiosyncrasies, and ease of editing by retyping a page encouraged more iterative drafting. The typewriter also contributed to the standardization of document formats: business letters, memos, and forms became more uniform as writers followed shared conventions for margins, line spacing, and punctuation.
The Rise of Electric Typewriters

By the mid-twentieth century, manufacturers sought to reduce the physical effort required for typing and increase speed through electrification. Electric typewriters used motors to assist keystrokes, making it easier to produce consistent impressions on the page and enabling additional features such as automatic carriage return.

The most iconic electric typewriter was IBM's Selectric, introduced in #. Instead of individual typebars, the Selectric employed a spherical "typeball" that tilted and rotated to bring the desired character into position before striking the paper.
Figure #: IBM Selectric II

This mechanism increased reliability and reduced jams. It also allowed users to swap the typeball, effectively changing the typeface on a single machine. This flexibility foreshadowed the font menus of digital word processors: typists could choose between different styles, such as serif and sans serif designs, by replacing a physical component.
Electric typewriters also integrated with early computing systems. Hybrid machines such as IBM's MT/ST (Magnetic Tape/Selectric Typewriter) combined a typewriter keyboard and print mechanism with magnetic tape storage, allowing documents to be recorded, edited, and reprinted. These systems bridged the gap between purely mechanical typewriters and fully electronic word processors.
From Word Processors to Digital Keyboards

In the #s and #s, dedicated word-processing machines and personal computers began to replace standalone typewriters in offices. Word processors offered transformative advantages: users could edit text on a screen before printing, store documents on disk, copy and paste passages, and apply more sophisticated formatting. Software such as WordStar, WordPerfect, and later Microsoft Word popularized these capabilities and made them accessible to a broad audience.
Figure #: Microsoft Word #.# for DOS (#)

As computers became standard office equipment, the role of the typewriter diminished. By the late twentieth century, most professional documents were created digitally. Yet the conceptual legacy of typewriting persisted. Computer keyboards largely adopted the typewriter's physical layout and QWERTY arrangement, preserving continuity in user skills. Even the language of computing reflects this heritage: we still speak of "typing" an email or "backspacing" to delete characters.
Today, typewriters occupy a niche as collectors' items, artistic tools, and symbols of a more tactile, deliberate approach to writing. Some authors and artists choose mechanical typewriters precisely because they lack the infinite undo and distraction-rich environment of digital devices. Meanwhile, the mainstream of text production has shifted to laptops, tablets, and phones, where virtual keyboards and predictive text further abstract the act of typewriting.
Digital Typewriting and the Evolution of Fonts

If the mechanical typewriter standardized letterforms on paper, digital typography exploded the possibilities for letter design on screen and in print. Early computer systems offered only a limited set of bitmap fonts, but the introduction of scalable outline fonts such as Adobe's PostScript Type # and Apple's TrueType allowed letters to be rendered at any size with smooth curves. The OpenType format, co-developed by Adobe and Microsoft, further extended this model by adding advanced layout features and support for large character sets.

OpenType fonts can store thousands of glyphs, including ligatures, small caps, stylistic alternates, and historical letterforms. Designers can use OpenType features to substitute glyphs contextually: for instance, replacing a pair of letters with a ligature that improves spacing or activating historical forms to evoke a particular period. This capability goes far beyond what was possible with a single, fixed set of metal type or a typewriter typebasket.
Digital typewriting also changed the economics of distribution. Instead of purchasing a physical machine with a single built-in typeface, designers and writers now license fonts separately. Online foundries and marketplaces offer thousands of type families, from workhorse text faces to experimental display designs. This abundance makes typographic choice a central part of visual communication in branding, user interfaces, and editorial design.

Variable Fonts: A New Frontier in Letter Design

One of the most important developments in contemporary typography is the rise of variable fonts. Variable fonts are OpenType font files that can store continuous ranges of design variations such as weight, width, and slant within a single file. Instead of shipping separate fonts for Light, Regular, Bold, Condensed, and Expanded styles, a typedesigner can encode these as axes in one variable font. Applications and web browsers can then interpolate smoothly between styles.
Figure #: Different styles on a complex font - source: Google fonts

Technically, variable fonts are based on the OpenType Font Variations mechanism, introduced into the OpenType specification in #. This technology allows software to select any instance along one or more axes of variation. For example, a designer might set body text at an intermediate weight and width that are not available as discrete fonts in a traditional family. On the web, variable fonts offer performance advantages because one file can replace many; in some experiments, consolidating dozens of styles into a single variable font has yielded substantial reductions in total font file size.
Variable fonts also open creative possibilities. Designers can animate typographic properties in response to user interaction letters that grow heavier on hover, or headlines that subtly expand as the viewport widens. They can encode custom axes for more experimental effects, such as the amount of serif, the roundness of terminals, or even the "mood" of a display typeface. In this way, variable fonts turn type design from a static set of snapshots into a parametric design space.
Color Fonts and Multicolored Letterforms

Another frontier in contemporary type design is the emergence of color fonts. Traditional digital fonts describe letter contours and rely on external color settings; a glyph is drawn as a monochrome outline that software fills with a single color. Color fonts, by contrast, embed color information directly in the font file. Technologies such as OpenType-SVG, COLR/CPAL, and CBDT/CBLC allow glyphs to include vector shapes with gradients, layered color planes, or even bitmap textures.

Color fonts enable rich typographic effects that previously required hand-drawn artwork or raster images. Designers can create letterforms that resemble neon signs, watercolor lettering, or layered printmaking, while preserving the benefits of text: scalability, searchability, and accessibility. Color fonts are increasingly supported in operating systems, design software, and modern browsers, although support remains uneven in some environments.
In parallel, emoji fonts represent a specialized form of color typography. They package thousands of colorful pictograms as font glyphs, allowing messaging apps and websites to render expressive icons using the same underlying systems that handle text. From this perspective, the typist of today may not only compose words but also blend them with tiny illustrations that communicate emotion and context.

Contemporary Typographic Trends

The tools provided by OpenType, variable fonts, and color fonts have catalyzed a rich diversity of design trends. In branding and editorial design, geometric sans serif typefaces remain popular for their clarity and modern feel. At the same time, there has been a resurgence of high-contrast serifs, script faces, and Art Nouveau–inspired display types that feature delicate ligatures and organic curves.
On the web, variable fonts support responsive typography: designers can adjust weight, width, and optical size to optimize reading across different screens. This allows a single type family to serve both dense body text on mobile and expansive headlines on large displays without compromising consistency. In interfaces, highly legible sans serif faces coexist with more expressive display fonts used sparingly to signal brand personality.
Another notable trend is the blending of historical references with contemporary technology. Some typefaces include OpenType features that activate historical forms such as the long "s" or blackletter-inspired shapes so that designers can create period atmospheres while still benefiting from modern rendering, hinting, and multilingual character coverage. Other families embrace brutalist or "incorrect" aesthetics, deliberately exaggerating contrast or disrupting conventional proportions to create memorable, attention-grabbing headlines.
The Continuing Influence of Typewriting

Although mechanical typewriters are no longer the dominant writing technology, their influence persists in both hardware and software. The standard computer keyboard layout, including the QWERTY arrangement and the staggered rows of keys, descends directly from nineteenth-century typewriter designs. Common interaction metaphors carriage return, backspace, tab derive from their mechanical counterparts, even if their implementations are now purely digital.
The typewriter has also become an aesthetic reference. Many digital fonts imitate the uneven ink distribution and slight misalignment of mechanical type, appealing to designers who want to evoke authenticity, nostalgia, or bureaucratic formality. In visual culture, typewriters symbolize seriousness, creativity, or vintage style, appearing frequently in films, advertisements, and social media imagery.
In another sense, today's AI-assisted writing tools can be seen as distant descendants of typewriters. While mechanical typewriters focused on making the act of writing more efficient, modern tools also assist with grammar, style, and even content generation. Yet at the center of this expanding technological ecosystem is the same basic act: pressing keys to turn thoughts into visible language.

Conclusion

From the clacking keys of the Remington No. # to the smooth animations of variable fonts on a high-resolution display, the story of typewriting is one of continuity and transformation. The earliest typewriters mechanized writing, making text production faster, more legible, and more standardized. Electric typewriters and word processors further increased efficiency and flexibility, while computers and digital typography unlocked a nearly infinite space of typographic variation.
Today, sophisticated letter designs enabled by OpenType features, variable fonts, color glyph technologies, and a global ecosystem of type designers allow text to carry nuanced voice and personality, even as it remains grounded in centuries-old alphabetic traditions. In this sense, we are still typewriting, even if the machine sits in the cloud rather than on the desk. The tools have changed dramatically, but the desire to shape written language through careful control of letterforms remains as strong as ever.
